findings.title: Denial cache short-circuits before the DB refresh, so a fresh grant is ignored for up to 30s
findings.body: Check() returns a cached deny as soon as the denial key is present, before it tries the cached permissions or re-queries the DB. The denial entry is written from a fresh DB result (line 154) but is never invalidated when permissions are granted. Sequence: user U checks dashboard X and is denied (denial entry stored, 30s TTL); U is then granted access to X (or X is created by U and U gets access); U checks X again within 30s. The denial hit returns Allowed=false, so the new 'requery DB when the resource is not in cached permissions' fallback never runs. That is exactly the 'creator cannot access what they just created' symptom this PR is meant to fix, and the denial cache re-introduces a stale-deny window that the fallback removed. The same applies to name-less checks (create flows, where the result only depends on whether any permission exists for the action). No test covers denial-then-grant.

findings.title: "Should deny on explicit cache deny entry" passes even if the denial cache is ignored
findings.body: The test is meant to prove that the denial cache short-circuits the check. But the permCache entry it sets is {"dashboards:uid:dash1": false}, a deny, so the cached-permission path also denies. The fallback then reads the DB, where setupService's fakeStore has no permissions, so it denies too. Removing the permDenialCache lookup in Check() leaves this test green. The comment on line 981 ('Allow access ... to prove this is not checked') contradicts the value set. There is also no test that a denial is written after a DB deny and then bypassed once the permission exists.

findings.title: Denial cache key is ambiguous because '_' separates fields that can contain '_'
findings.body: userPermDenialCacheKey joins namespace, user UID, action, name and parent with '_', and Grafana UIDs and names often contain underscores. Different tuples collide: name "a_b" with parent "c" and name "a" with parent "b_c" both produce "...perm_<uid>_<action>_a_b_c". If the first is denied and cached, the second (which the user may be allowed) is wrongly denied for the 30s TTL. The key needs an unambiguous encoding (length prefix, escaping or a hash).

findings.title: Every DB denial is cached under a request-controlled key with no size bound
findings.body: The denial key is built from the request's name and parent folder, and an entry is written for every denied request. The local cache used here (authlib cache.NewLocalCache) has no size cap in its configuration. A user can issue requests with many distinct names (including nonexistent ones) and fill the cache with entries for 30s each. Denial entries also add a write per denied request on top of the DB query. A bounded cache or a cap on what is cached would limit this.

findings.title: Failed user lookup is performed twice per request in Check and List
findings.body: getCachedIdentityPermissions calls GetUserIdentifiers, and its error is then ignored. The fallback getIdentityPermissions path calls GetUserIdentifiers again. Failed lookups are not cached, so for an unknown or deleted user every request issues two identical DB queries (Check at line 123 then line 139; List at lines 180 and 186). The identifier lookup should be done once and reused.

findings.title: Remote/cloud client still keeps the 30s authlib client cache, so the stale-result symptom remains there
findings.body: The PR removes the authlib client cache only for the in-proc client (ProvideAuthZClient). newRemoteRBACClient still wraps the client in a 30s LocalCache, which caches Check results on the client side. A creator using a remote or standalone authz server will therefore still see stale results for a newly created resource for up to 30s, regardless of the server-side fallback. The PR description only mentions in-proc, so either this is intentional and should be documented, or the remote path is not fixed.
